summary: Redwood Optimize walkthrough focusing on quantization profiles (INT8 vs FP8). SE demoed tooling that recommends profiles by workload, tradeoffs across quality, latency, and cost, and showed example benchmarks on Acme-like prompts. Customer is interested in a short pilot to validate FP8 quality on clinical summarization prompts and compare latency/cost to INT8 and hosted variants.
topics: Optimize tool recommendations and profile tuning
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-12-18
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~54 minutes
Attendees: Sophie Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Ramos (Redwood SE), Maya Patel (Acme CTO), Evan Lopez (Acme ML Eng), Priya Singh (Acme Security)

[00:00] Sophie: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, quick intro. I m Sophie, AE on the Redwood side, Diego SE will lead the optimize walkthrough. How s everyone doing?
[00:08] Maya: Doing well, thanks. We re excited to see the quantization stuff, we've been hearing about FP8 a lot.
[00:13] Diego: Great. Quick agenda: we ll show the Optimize console, quantization profiles, how we measure quality vs latency, then walk through a couple of sample benchmarks and discuss pilot next steps.
[00:22] Evan: Sounds good. Our main goal is to see whether FP8 will keep clinical summarization quality for our notes workflows while reducing cost and keeping latency under 300ms for 512 tokens.
[00:35] Priya: And I have some security questions later about KMS and audit logs.
[00:40] Diego: Perfect, will cover that briefly at the end.

[01:05] Diego: Ok sharing screen - Console - Optimize tab. Apologies if the screen name shows "Redwood Optimise" in the demo tenant, old spelling from a demo build, ignore that.
[01:16] Sophie: Typical in demos, yes.

[01:30] Diego: First, the quantization profiles UI. We have prebuilt profiles: FP16 baseline, INT8, FP8-mix, plus conservative/quality-first and latency-first presets. The profiler recommends a starting profile based on tokens distribution and model arch (we detect seq-lens and kv-cache patterns).
[01:50] Evan: How automated is that? Do you run a micro-benchmark on our sample?
[01:55] Diego: Yes, the suggestion step runs a small calibration set — usually a few hundred prompts — to estimate token-level MSE and downstream metric delta. It s lightweight; we can run it in a couple of minutes.

[02:15] [Diego moves to benchmark screen] Here s an example on a 7B open model (we re using a curated community model). The dashboard shows three axes: latency, cost per 1k tokens, and a quality delta bar (ROUGE/BLEU or a custom eval).
[02:35] Maya: In that screenshot I see FP8 near-parity with FP16 on ROUGE but half the cost vs baseline, is that real?
[02:42] Diego: For that workload yes — that s common for summarization style prompts where quantization noise doesn t strongly affect decoding. Caveat: sensitive tasks like fact extraction or numeric precision can show differing behaviour.

[03:05] Evan: What about INT8? We re seeing a lot of claims that INT8 is best for latency on some hardware.
[03:12] Diego: INT8 tends to give fastest kernel runtime on some GPUs and quant libraries, but it s more aggressive in representational loss. We give you a profile that balances per-layer quant scale, per-channel calibrations, and can leave critical layers in FP16. So INT8 often wins cost and latency but you have to validate quality.

[03:40] [04:00] Diego: Here s a barrel of sample runs — FP16 baseline: avg latency 420ms, FP8: 280ms, INT8: 240ms, cost per 1k tokens scaling accordingly. But our quality signal shows FP8 delta at -0.8% ROUGE, INT8 delta at -3.4% for this dataset.
[04:25] Maya: Those numbers line up with our internal pilot on a nonclinical data set. For clinical notes even a small drop can be concerning.
[04:33] Diego: Totally. That s why our optimize flow includes evaluation hooks so you can plug in your own rubric — e.g., clinical accuracy or hallucination checks. We also provide sample-level diffs so you can inspect where outputs diverged.

[04:55] Evan: Can you show how we can pin layers to avoid quantizing them?
[05:02] Diego: Yep — in the profile editor you can toggle layer groups: attention, feedforward, embedding. For clinical summarization we often recommend keeping the first embedding and last decoder FFN in FP16; the tool suggests those based on sensitivity heuristics.

[05:30] [05:45] Diego: There s also the continuous rollout option — you can start traffic at 5% FP8, trace quality metrics, and rollback automatically if a metric breaches. We call that a canary with automatic fallback to baseline model or to another region.
[06:00] Maya: We d want the automatic rollback. We can t risk production regressions.
[06:05] Sophie: We ll include rollback SLOs in the pilot.

[06:22] Evan: On hardware: we run NVIDIA H100 on-prem for some workloads. How similar are your kernels on cloud vs our H100?
[06:31] Diego: We compile kernels per-hardware; for H100 FP8 kernels are generally well optimized but there s nuance between driver versions. We ll run the same compiled kernels in your environment for the pilot to ensure parity. Small differences can appear in perf numbers but not usually in quality.

[06:55] Priya: Security: KMS and audit logs. We need to ensure keys never leave our VPC and there are immutable audit events for any model changes.
[07:03] Diego: For Redwood Private we support customer-managed KMS and HSM integrations; audit logs are exported to your SIEM. We ll send the SOC2 docs and KMS integration notes after this call.
[07:15] Priya: Great. Also residency: our data needs to stay in US-East for now.
[07:19] Sophie: Noted — we have region pinning in Dedicated and Private.

[07:30] [07:45] Diego: Back to bench examples — I ll open the sample diff viewer. Here s an FP8 vs FP16 pair where FP8 introduced a subtle paraphrase that changes a medical assertion; the viewer highlights and lets you trace logits/n-best. You can then mark that as a regression and exclude similar inputs or pin layers to avoid that class of error.
[08:10] Evan: That inspection tooling is key for us. If we can triage and mark false positives quickly it makes pilot evaluation much faster.

[08:30] Diego: We also have automatic thresholding: you set acceptable delta on your primary metric, and the rollout will stop or rollback if it s exceeded.

[08:45] Maya: What about cost math — can you show a real example with our projected throughput?
[08:50] Sophie: We did a quick model for you — Evan shared sample traffic — we estimate for 10M tokens/mo FP16 baseline is $X, FP8 reduces by ~45%, INT8 reduces by ~55% depending on kernel and batching. We ll include that spreadsheet.

[09:20] Evan: Is there an API flow to trigger re-profiling if our prompt sets change?
[09:25] Diego: Yes, there s an API and a console button to re-run the suggestor on a new trace. It can be scheduled nightly for continuous tuning.

[09:40] [10:00] Maya: A few practical questions — does quantization affect embedding generation or only decoding?
[10:06] Diego: We support quantizing encoder and decoder paths; for embeddings we often keep precision higher because downstream retrieval sensitivity can be high. But you can profile embedding distance deltas in the tool.

[10:25] Evan: For our evaluation can we run both INT8 and FP8 on the same machine concurrently to compare latency?
[10:30] Diego: Yes, our runtime supports multiple profile variants; for a fair perf comparison we usually run them in isolation to avoid scheduling noise but the tool can orchestrate controlled experiments.

[10:50] Diego: ...walking through the Optimize API — code snippet shows how to create a profile, pass in sample prompts and metrics, and start a compare job.
[11:10] [11:40] Diego (slightly mumbled): Note that KV cache behavior matters a lot — we saw in one workload that prefix caching reduced token compute by 35% which changes the lat vs cost tradeoff. Sometimes transcription shows "KV cash" in older notes.
[11:55] Sophie: Diego s jokes aside, caching is big.

[12:10] Evan: What should success criteria for the pilot look like?
[12:15] Sophie: We recommend: 1) FP8 quality delta < 1.0% on your clinical metric, 2) median latency < 300ms for 512 tokens, 3) cost reduction >= 40% vs FP16, and 4) no critical regressions in 500-sample spot checks.
[12:35] Maya: Those look reasonable. We might require a slightly tighter quality delta; we ll specify after Evan runs the prompt set.

[12:50] Priya: On legal/comms, we need a data processing addendum. Can you send contract docs?
[12:55] Sophie: Yes we ll loop in legal, send DPA and SOC2.

[13:10] Diego: Quick demo of the rollout UI — set a canary, auto-metrics, manual approval gates, and automatic rollback. We also show traces and per-token latency heatmap.
[13:35] Evan: Nice.

[13:50] [14:05] Diego: Ok recapping next steps: Sophie will send pricing and the quant benchmark spreadsheet; Evan will share prompt sets; Diego will schedule runs and provide results; Priya will list security questions.
[14:20] Maya: Thanks all. Any other questions?
[14:25] Evan: No, looks good.
[14:30] Sophie: Thanks everyone, we ll follow up with calendar invites for the pilot kickoff.

[54:00] End of call

Notes on transcription: occasional mis-attrs and minor audio dropouts around 00:55; some product names mis-typed (Optimise vs Optimize), and NVidia spelled sometimes as "N V I D I A" — transcription quality set to medium.
